Form
form
n. (shape, outward appearance; also the essential nature of a thing; rendering Hebrew to'ar, tohu in the negative, Greek morphe, morphosis)
From Latin forma, shape. The Greek distinction Scripture exploits is between morphe, the form that expresses what a thing truly is, and morphosis, the mere outline or appearance of it — and Paul uses both, of Christ and of hypocrites.

Biblical Definition

Form in Scripture ranges from bare shape to essential nature, and the most weighty use is Paul's in the Philippian hymn. Christ was in the form of God and “made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men” (Philippians 2:7). The Greek morphe is not costume; it is the outward expression of what a thing genuinely is, which is why the same word can describe His deity and His servanthood without making either a disguise. He did not appear to be God and then appear to be a servant; He was both, and the second was assumed without the first being laid down. Isaiah's servant song sets the paradox in advance: “he hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him” (Isaiah 53:2). Paul then uses the shallower cognate for religion that is all outline: men “having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away” (2 Timothy 3:5) — morphosis, the shape without the substance. And the verb governs the Christian's transformation: “be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind” (Romans 12:2), where the world presses a shape from outside and the Spirit works one from within, at the mind.

Webster 1828 Definition

Shape, and also essential nature. Christ was in the form of God and took the form of a servant — expression of what He truly is, not costume; the last days have a form of godliness without its power; and the Christian is transformed rather than conformed.

FORM, n. [L. forma.] The shape or external appearance of a body; the figure, as defined by lines and angles.

2. Manner of arranging particulars; disposition of particular things.

3. Model; draught; pattern.

4. Beauty; elegance; splendor; dignity. He hath no form nor comeliness. Is. 53.

5. Stated method; established practice; ritual or prescribed mode; as the forms of public worship. A form of godliness. 2 Tim. 3.

Key Scripture

Philippians 2:7 — "But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men:"

Isaiah 53:2 — "For he shall grow up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground: he hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him."

2 Timothy 3:5 — "Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away."

Romans 12:2 — "And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God."

Modern Corruption

2 Timothy 3:5 is turned against form as such — liturgy, order, and set prayers dismissed as dead formalism — when Paul's complaint is a form emptied of power, not the existence of a form.

expand to see more

“A form of godliness, but denying the power thereof” is the standing proof-text for a spontaneity that suspects all structure: written prayers are insincere, an order of service quenches the Spirit, and confession recited is confession unfelt. Paul is not making that argument. His subject in 2 Timothy 3 is a catalogue of vices — lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, without natural affection, traitors — held by men who nonetheless keep the outward shape of religion. The problem is the vice, not the shape; and a man of that description is no less dangerous for praying extempore. Scripture is in fact full of prescribed forms: a form of words for the priestly blessing, a psalter for sung worship, and a set prayer given by the Lord Himself with the words when ye pray, say. The regulative principle the dictionary holds is not hostility to form but the conviction that God appoints the forms of His own worship.

The opposite error is the one Paul is actually addressing, and it wears better clothes. A church may hold the confession, keep the calendar, sing the psalms, and administer the ordinances, and be dead — and the outward correctness makes the deadness harder to see, both from outside and from within. This is why the same Scripture that gives the forms insists relentlessly on the reality: circumcision of the heart and not the flesh, a broken and contrite heart rather than sacrifice, the Sabbath kept while the poor are ground. Paul's prescription is not reform of the liturgy but separation from the men — from such turn away. The remedy for a form without power has never been the abolition of the form; it is the return of the power, which is not in the church's gift to manufacture and must be sought where it is given.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew to'ar (form, outline, comeliness) and tohu (formlessness); Greek morphe (the form expressing essential nature), morphosis (an outline or semblance), and metamorphoo (to transform).

expand to see more

Hebrew to'ar (H8389) — form, outline, figure; the word in Isaiah 53:2 and of Joseph and Rachel being well favoured.

Greek morphe (G3444) — form as the expression of essential nature; used twice in Philippians 2:6-7, of God and of a servant.

Greek morphosis (G3446) — a forming, semblance, outline; the word in 2 Timothy 3:5 and Romans 2:20.

Greek metamorphoo (G3339) — to transform, transfigure; used of Christ on the mount and of the believer in Romans 12:2 and 2 Corinthians 3:18.

Greek syschematizo (G4964) — to conform to a pattern, fashion oneself after; the verb in Romans 12:2 rendered conformed.

Usage

"“The form of a servant” — morphe, the expression of what He truly became, not a costume worn."

"“He hath no form nor comeliness” — nothing in the appearance to account for what He was."

"“A form of godliness, but denying the power” — the shape kept and the substance gone."
